pool.q: What medication causes corneal melting?
pool.rationale:
Ketorolac (Acular) is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to treat postoperative inflammation and allergic conjunctivitis. Other topical NSAIDs include diclofenac sodium (Voltaren), flurbiprofen sodium (Ocufen), nepafenac (Nevanac), and bromfenac sodium (Xibrom). The NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase in the metabolism of arachidonic acid. Diclofenac and ketorolac have been associated with corneal melting and perforation. Although all topical NSAIDs can theoretically cause these complications, the vast majority of cases were found with generic diclofenac, which was subsequently removed from the US market. Caution must be used in patients using these medications and especially patients with pre-existing ocular surface disease or diabetes.
Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antimicrobial that binds reversibly to the 50S ribosomal subunit. It can be used to treat eye infections with H influenzae, N gonorrhoeae, N meningitides, and all anaerobic bacteria. It has some activity against Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter and Serratia species, S pneumoniae, and S aureus. A major side effect is idiosyncratic aplastic anemia. Nedocromil (Alocril) and azelastine HCl (Optivar) are combination mast cell stabilizers and H1 antagonists. They are used to prevent the acute release of histamine and degranulation of mast cells in the treatment of allergic symptoms. They are not associated with corneal melting.

pool.q: What morphogen interacts with intracellular receptors to regulate gene expression during eye development?
pool.rationale: External signals (morphogens) are required to guide appropriate development of embryonic eye cells. Morphogens can be divided into 2 broad groups. Group 1 ligands (retinoic acid) bind to intracellular receptors and directly affect gene expression. Group 2 ligands (fibroblast growth factor, Wnt, and sonic hedgehog) impact gene expression by binding to extracellular receptors and triggering a cascade that eventually also impacts gene expression. Importantly, cells can have a different fate depending on which morphogen they are exposed to. Also, the relative concentration of the morphogens (morphogenic gradient) impacts the differentiation of cells.

pool.q: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum are at increased risk for which ocular cancers?

options.a: squamous cell carcinoma and choroidal melanoma
options.c: squamous cell carcinoma and ocular surface melanoma

pool.rationale: Xeroderma pigmentosum is a severe condition caused by a genetic mutation that affects DNA repair enzymes. Patients with this disorder have diffuse pigmented anomalies on their sun-exposed skin and are at high risk for squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma of the ocular surface. Their risks of choroidal melanoma and retinoblastoma are not increased.

pool.q: What medication has been implicated in outbreaks of contamination-related infectious endophthalmitis?
pool.rationale:
Aflibercept (Eylea), bevacizumab (Avastin), pegaptanib sodium (Macugen), and ranibizumab (Lucentis) are anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents used to treat neovascular age-related macular degeneration, macular edema due to diabetes, and retinal vein occlusion, and other eye conditions. Aflibercept, pegaptanib sodium, and ranibizumab are sterilely packaged in single-use containers and are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for several ophthalmic indications. In contrast, bevacizumab, which is molecularly related to ranibizumab, is not FDA approved for ophthalmic indications. However, it is routinely packaged at compounding pharmacies and administered intravitreally for ophthalmic conditions because it costs less than any of the FDA-approved anti-VEGF agents.
Administering a medication for indications other than those for which it was approved by the FDA is referred to as "off label" use. In 2011, outbreaks of endophthalmitis related to compounded bevacizumab led the American Academy of Ophthalmology to issue new guidelines to help ensure the safety and sterility of compounded medications. Understanding which medications are compounded and which are used off-label is important for clinicians in guiding informed consent and patient-care related discussions.

pool.q: Where does cranial nerve III (CN III) typically separate into superior and inferior divisions?
pool.rationale: Cranial nerve III (CN III) usually separates into superior and inferior divisions after passing through the annulus of Zinn in the orbit. Both the superior and inferior divisions pass through the superior orbital fissure within the annulus. However, in some individuals, CN III divides within the anterior cavernous sinus. The optic canal carries the optic nerve through the annulus of Zinn. CN III maintains a topographic organization even in the midbrain, so lesions almost anywhere along its course may cause a divisional nerve palsy. The superior division of CN III innervates the superior rectus and levator palpebrae muscles. The larger inferior division splits into 3 branches to supply the medial rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. Parasympathetic pupillary fibers also course along the inferior division of CN III to enter the orbit and synapse with the ciliary ganglion.

pool.q: The parasympathetic fibers travel with what nerve fibers to reach the ciliary ganglion?

options.a: the inferior division of the third cranial nerve (CN III)
options.b: the superior division of the third cranial nerve (CN III)
options.c: the lacrimal nerve of the fifth cranial nerve (CN V1)
options.d: the frontal nerve of the fifth cranial nerve (CN V1)

pool.rationale: Parasympathetic fibers that travel with CN III reach the ciliary ganglion via the inferior division of CN III when it splits into superior and inferior divisions. The ciliary ganglion is located in the orbit, situated on the lateral surface of the ophthalmic artery lateral to the optic nerve and medial to the lateral rectus muscle, approximately 1 cm in front of the orbital apex. Parasympathetic fibers destined to synapse in the ciliary ganglion travel with CN III. When CN III splits into superior and inferior divisions, the parasympathetics travel with the inferior division to reach the ciliary ganglion. Sympathetic fibers pass through the ganglion, but do not synapse there.

pool.q: Which extraocular muscle originates from the annulus of Zinn?
pool.rationale: The annulus of Zinn consists of superior and inferior orbital tendons and is the origin of the 4 rectus muscles. The upper tendon gives rise to the entire superior rectus muscle, as well as portions of the lateral and medial rectus muscles. The inferior tendon gives rise to the entire inferior rectus muscle and portions of the medial and lateral rectus muscles. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle arises from the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, at the apex of the orbit, just superior to the annulus of Zinn.

pool.q: Soft contact lenses with low oxygen permeability cause corneal edema via the accumulation of what substance?
pool.rationale:
Under anaerobic (low-oxygen) conditions, glucose, the main metabolic substrate for the cornea, is converted to pyruvic acid and then to lactic acid. Lactic acid accumulation in the stroma increases the osmotic load, which draws water into the cornea and causes corneal edema.
Carbon dioxide, aldehyde dehydrogenase, and proteoglycans do not accumulate in the cornea in hypoxic conditions. Carbon dioxide is a product of glucose metabolism via glycolysis under aerobic conditions. Aldehyde dehydrogenase is a soluble protein found in the cornea that absorbs ultraviolet B (UVB) light. Proteoglycans confer hydrophilic properties to the corneal stroma and interact with collagen fibrils to provide corneal clarity.

pool.q: What is the highest percentage of a topically administered eye drop retained in an upright blinking patient?

pool.q: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) block prostaglandin biosynthesis by inhibition of what enzyme?
pool.rationale: The production of eicosanoids, which include prostaglandins, leukotrienes, prostacyclin, and thromboxane, is important to understand. Prostaglandins (PGs) are especially relevant to the eye, as they impact aqueous humor dynamics, affect the blood-ocular barrier, and can cause miosis. This important cascade starts with the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2, an enzyme blocked by corticosteroids. Freed arachidonic acid can then be converted to prostaglandins by cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) or -2 (COX-2). Thromboxane synthetase acts further "downstream," converting primary PGs to thromboxane, which is a potent vasoconstrictor and platelet-aggregating agent. Alternative to PG synthesis, lipoxygenase can convert free arachidonic acid to leukotrienes. Topical and systemic NSAIDs block prostaglandin (PG) synthesis by the irreversible binding of cyclooxygenase (COX).

pool.q: What is the primary source of glucose for the corneal stroma?
pool.rationale: The stroma receives glucose primarily from the aqueous humor by carrier-mediated transport through the endothelium; the epithelium receives glucose by passive diffusion through the stroma and from the tear film. The precorneal tear film and limbal vessels supply approximately 10% of the glucose used by the cornea.

pool.q: What cycloplegic has the longest duration of action?
pool.rationale:
For uveitis, topical mydriatic and cycloplegic agents are used to prevent posterior synechiae and to relieve pain due to ciliary spasm.
Atropine sulfate has the longest duration of action (7-14 days), followed by scopolamine (4-7 days), homatropine (3 days), and cyclopentolate (2 days).

pool.q: Which cranial nerve also carries innervation to the pupillary sphincter muscle?
pool.rationale: Cranial nerve III carries cholinergic innervation to the pupillary sphincter muscles. Patients with impingement on CN III (for example, those with an aneurysm) will have abnormal pupillary function in addition to oculomotor deficits. Although the post-ganglionic neurons of parasympathetic ganglia travel with branches of the trigeminal nerve, CN V is not part of the cranial outflow of the parasympathetic nervous system.

pool.q: What is the outer layer of the tear film in the 2-phase model?

pool.q: An unaffected woman has a brother, maternal uncle, and son affected with retinitis pigmentosa. What is the most likely mode of inheritance?

pool.q: What feature of the retinal pigment epithelium contributes to the blood-retina barrier?

options.a: polarized distribution of ion channels and transporters

pool.rationale: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) has multiple structural specializations that underlie its support of the function and health of the neurosensory retina. Tight junctions located in the lateral surfaces of adjacent RPE form the outer blood-retina barrier. The differing apical versus basal distributions of ion channels and transporters support the dehydrated state of the subretinal space. The envelopment of the photoreceptor outer segments by the RPE apical microvilli facilitates the phagocytosis of shed discs as well as the renewal of visual pigments needed for the visual cycle. Melanosomes absorb light.

pool.q: What abnormality of embryologic development is responsible for the formation of optic nerve colobomas?

options.b: incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure
options.c: incomplete regression of the primary vitreous
options.d: failed induction of the surface ectoderm lens placode

pool.rationale:
Optic nerve coloboma results from defective closure of the posterior embryonic or choroidal fissure. It occurs inferonasally in the optic nerve head and is associated with colobomatous defects of other tissues along the embryonic fissure, including retina and choroid, ciliary body, and iris.

Failure of neural crest differentiation profoundly affects development of the ocular structures and results in cryptophthalmos (absence of the eyelids, conjunctiva, cornea, and lens). The primary vitreous consists of fibrillar material, mesenchymal cells, and vascular components.

The tunica vasculosa lentis surrounds the developing lens, the vasa hyaloidea propria is a network of vessels posterior to the lens, and the hyaloid artery connects the vasa hyaloidea propria to the optic nerve. Failure of these vessels to regress results in persistent fetal vasculature and often microphthalmia. Early in embryogenesis, the optic vesicle influences the specific region of head ectoderm to form the lens placode. The lens placode later invaginates to become the lens vesicle. If there is failure of induction of the lens placode, the lens never develops. This is primary congenital aphakia and is associated with mutations in PAX6. Other severe ocular and systemic abnormalities also occur.

pool.q: The adverse effects of reactive oxygen species (ROS) have been repeatedly proposed as causal factors in what ocular disease?
pool.rationale: The adverse effects of ROS have been repeatedly proposed as causal factors in many vision-threatening diseases, including cataract, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy, and glaucoma. Lipid peroxides are formed when ROS react with unsaturated fatty acids. The oxidation of membrane phospholipids has been hypothesized to increase the permeability of cell membranes, which contributes eventually to cell malfunction and potentially to cell lysis.

pool.q: What geographic zone of the conjunctiva adheres firmly to the tarsus?
pool.rationale: The conjunctiva can be divided into 3 geographic zones: palpebral, forniceal, and bulbar. The palpebral conjunctiva begins at the mucocutaneous junction of the eyelid and covers the lid's inner surface This part adheres firmly to the tarsus. The forniceal conjunctiva is the zone that is freely movable and redundant in the fornices. It becomes enmeshed with fibrous elements of the levator aponeurosis and Müller muscle in the upper eyelid and with fibrous expansions of the inferior rectus muscle sheath, which fuse with the inferior tarsal muscle in the lower lid. The bulbar conjunctiva fuses with the Tenon capsule and inserts into the limbus. There is no superficial zone of conjunctiva.

pool.q: In what vitreous-associated process has age-related loss of type IX collagen been implicated?

options.b: increased diffusion of oxygen from the anterior segment into the posterior segment

pool.rationale: Vitreous liquefaction, also known as syneresis, begins with the breakdown of collagen fibrils into smaller fragments. This liquefaction is thought to occur because of a loss of shielding of type II collagen by type IX collagen. This process has no direct effect on the development of vitreous hemorrhage unless it leads to the development of posterior vitreous detachment (PVD). A PVD can protect against retinal neovascularization by eliminating the scaffold for fibrovascular proliferation. Oxygen tension increases in the posterior chamber in postvitrectomized eyes.

pool.q: In what eyelid structure do the insertion point of the orbital septum and the attachments to the skin create the variations in eyelid anatomy between many patients of Asian descent and patients of other races?
pool.rationale: In many individuals of Asian descent, there are few attachments of the levator aponeurosis to the skin near the upper tarsal border, and the superior eyelid fold is minimal or absent. In most non-Asian races, the orbital septum inserts onto the levator aponeurosis above the tarsus. In Asian eyelids, the orbital septum inserts into the levator aponeurosis between the eyelid margin and the superior border of the tarsus. The Müller muscle, orbicularis oculi, and tarsal plate do not account for any racial differences in Asian eyelid anatomy.

pool.q: What is the physiologic rate of endothelial cell loss with normal aging?
pool.rationale: The corneal endothelium, located posterior to the Descemet membrane, is a monolayer of hexagonal cells with a diameter of 20 µm. In young adults, the normal endothelial cell count is approximately 3000/mm2 centrally. The number of endothelial cells is higher in the periphery and decreases with age. There is a concomitant spreading and thinning of the remaining cells. The rate of physiologic corneal endothelial cell loss with normal aging has been reported to be 0.6% per year.

pool.q: What growth factors are implicated in the excessive proliferation of Tenon capsule fibroblasts that can scar a glaucoma filtration bleb?
pool.rationale: Transforming growth factor betas and platelet-derived growth factor are implicated in the excessive proliferation of Tenon capsule fibroblasts, which can result in scarring of the glaucoma filtration bleb. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is implicated in the pathogenesis of various retinovascular conditions. Insulin-like growth factor may be responsible for the abnormal hyperplastic response of the lens epithelium and corneal endothelium observed in inflammatory conditions. Fibroblast growth factors can accelerate corneal wound repair after surgery, chemical burns, or ulcers.

pool.q: The disruption of what cornea layer in laser subepithelial keratomileusis (LASEK) is thought to be the cause of increased risk for visual complications postoperatively due to central cornea haze?
pool.rationale: It is thought that the Bowman layer, by virtue of its acellularity and packing distribution, serves to prevent exposure of stromal corneal keratocytes to growth factors secreted by corneal epithelial cells. This effect is notable because during photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) or LASEK, the Bowman layer, along with the anterior corneal stromal tissue, is removed. In these procedures, corneal haze is a potentially significant postoperative visual complication, presumably because the stromal keratocytes are exposed to regenerating epithelial growth factors and take on fibroblastic behaviors. On the other hand, in laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), the Bowman layer is transected but still retained, and thus central cornea haze is extremely rare.

pool.q: What part of the corneal epithelium can cause recurrent corneal erosions if it does not re-form correctly after trauma?
pool.rationale: The anterior surface of the cornea is covered by a lipophilic, nonkeratinized, stratified squamous epithelium. The basal cell layer is attached to the basal lamina by hemidesmosomes. Recurrent corneal erosion from epithelial damage is due to improper reformation of the hemidesmosomes. Overlying the basal cell layer are 2 to 3 layers of polygonal wing cells. They are attached by tight junctions and are not related to recurrent erosions. Collagen fibrils make up the Bowman layer. Ground substance is part of the corneal stroma.

pool.q: What orbital surgical space contains the ciliary ganglion?
pool.rationale:
The orbit comprises 5 surgical spaces: subperiosteal, sub-Tenon, extraconal, intraconal, and subarachnoid.
The ciliary ganglion is found on the lateral surface of the optic nerve sheath, 1 centimeter anterior to the annulus of Zinn, in the orbital apex between the optic nerve and the lateral rectus muscle. Therefore, it is intraconal.
The only structures found in the subarachnoid space of the orbit are the optic nerve and the central retinal artery/vein.
Both the subperiosteal and sub-Tenon spaces contain no significant structures, although a variety of vessels pierce and pass through them. Both of these locations represent potential dead spaces where fluid may collect because of the loose adherence of the linings to the underlying anatomy (periosteum to bone and Tenon capsule to sclera), and they are relatively avascular.

pool.q: What is the sensory function of cranial nerve VII?

options.c: preganglionic sympathetic innervation of the ciliary ganglion
options.d: taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue

pool.rationale: Cranial nerve VII (the facial nerve) is a complex, mixed sensory and motor nerve. The motor root contains special visceral efferent fibers that innervate the muscles of facial expression. The sensory root conveys the sense of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and sensation from the external auditory meatus and the retroauricular skin. It also supplies preganglionic parasympathetic innervation by way of the sphenopalatine and submandibular ganglia to the lacrimal, submaxillary, and sublingual glands.

pool.rationale: Cyclosporine A, prednisolone acetate, matrix metalloproteinases, and doxycycline are all anti-inflammatory drugs that have been observed to improve the clinical symptoms of keratoconjunctivitis sicca/dry eye syndrome. pool.q: Into what structure do the lymphatics from the lateral upper eyelid palpebral conjunctiva drain?
pool.rationale: No lymphatic vessels or lymph nodes have been found in the orbit. It is suggested that all the orbital veins contain perivascular channels that may act similar to a lymphatic vessel. A medial group of lymphatic vessels drain the medial part of the eyelid and tear sac. They follow the path of the anterior facial vein and drain to the submandibular lymph nodes. A lateral group of lymphatic vessels drain the rest of the eyelid and drain into the superficial preauricular lymph nodes.

pool.q: In the normal physiologic human eye, what component of the aqueous is always higher in concentration in the aqueous than in plasma?
pool.rationale:
Aqueous is the major nutrient source for the avascular lens and cornea and provides a route for the removal of waste products. Ocular fluids are separated from blood by barriers formed by tight junctions between epithelial and endothelial cells. This makes up the blood-aqueous barrier. Aqueous enters the posterior chamber from the ciliary processes by means of active and passive physiologic mechanisms, resulting in specific concentrations of various ions to maintain a specific composition of the fluid. In order of highest to lowest concentration, the components of aqueous humor are (see Table 9-1):
  • Na+ (163 mmol/kg H2O)
  • Cl- (134 mmol/kg H2O)
  • HCO-3 (20 mmol/kg H2O)
  • Glucose (3 mmol/kg H2O)
  • Ascorbate (1.06 mmol/kg H2O).
Lactate is the most abundant organic anion in the aqueous, and its concentration in the aqueous is always higher than that in plasma. Calcium is generally 50% less concentrated in the aqueous versus plasma, and aqueous concentration of glucose is about 70% of the concentration found in plasma (can be higher in diabetics, leading to problems with refraction due to lens retention of glucose short-term, and cataract formation long-term). Urea's concentration in the aqueous is about 80%-90% of that in plasma.

pool.q: How do the high ascorbate levels in aqueous humor help protect intraocular structures?

options.c: They prevent diffusion of plasma proteins.

pool.rationale: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) levels in aqueous are much higher (some 10–50 times higher) than those in plasma. The high ascorbate level protects intraocular structures by blocking ultraviolet light. Glutathione removes excess hydrogen peroxide. Inositol is important for phospholipid synthesis. The tight junctions of the nonpigmented epithelium prevent diffusion of plasma proteins.

pool.q: What portion of the sclera is derived from mesoderm?
pool.rationale:
Neuroectoderm develops into the following structures:
  • retina
  • retinal pigment epithelium
  • pigmented ciliary epithelium
  • nonpigmented ciliary epithelium
  • pigmented iris epithelium
  • sphincter and dilator muscle of iris
  • optic nerve
  • vitreous

  • sclera except for temporal portion
  • trabecular meshwork
  • sheaths/tendons of extraocular muscles
  • connective tissue of iris
  • ciliary muscle
  • choroidal stroma
  • meningeal sheath of optic nerve
  • ciliary ganglion
  • muscle and connective tissue layer of all ocular and orbital vessels
Surface ectoderm develops into the following structures:
  • eyelid
  • cilia
  • eyelid glands
  • lacrimal gland
  • conjunctiva
  • lens
  • nasolacrimal duct
  • vitreous
Mesoderm develops into the following structures:
  • extraocular muscles
  • endothelium of vessels
  • temporal portion of sclera
  • vitreous

pool.q: What ocular structure receives its nutrition primarily from the aqueous humor?
pool.rationale: Aqueous humor provides nutrient support to avascular structures inside the eye, including the lens, trabecular meshwork, and cornea. Structures that are vascular receive their nutrient support via their internal blood supply.

pool.q: What condition would be a contraindication to use of systemic hyperosmotic agents?
pool.rationale:
Hyperosmotic agents, as well as oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, are contraindicated in patients in renal failure or on dialysis.
Adverse effects of hyperosmotic agents include headache, mental confusion, backache, acute congestive heart failure, and myocardial infarction. Subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhages have been reported after treatment with hyperosmotic agents.
Although carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are derived from sulfa drugs, sulfa allergy is not a contraindication to the administration of hyperosmotic agents, such as oral glycerol or intravenous mannitol.

pool.q: What cell population increases with the use of topical cyclosporine 0.05%?
pool.rationale:
Biopsies have demonstrated a measurable repopulation of goblet cells, and a decrease in conjunctival epithelial cell turnover and in the number of lymphocytes with use of topical cyclosporine 0.05% (Restasis). Patients reported fewer dry eye complaints at 6 months in initial studies.
Acinar cells are 1 of the 2 cell types within lacrimal glands, which are exocrine glands that produce serous secretion. Lacrimal glands also contain myoepithelial cells.
Sebaceous cells are present within the meibomian glands, glands of Zeis, and glands of the caruncle.

pool.q: What mechanism results in the random oxidation of lipids?
pool.rationale: Auto-oxidation is the mechanism by which random oxidation of lipids takes place. It is inhibited by free-radical scavengers such as vitamin E. Photo-oxidation is a process by which oxygen is activated electronically by light to form singlet oxygen. Lipid peroxidation causes not only direct damage to the cell membrane but also secondary damage in cells through its aldehydic breakdown products.

pool.q: What substance is combined with and activates fibrinogen to form the sealant in a fibrin-based tissue adhesive?
pool.rationale: Thrombin combines with fibrinogen to form a biological tissue adhesive. Thrombin is also used to control intraocular hemorrhage during vitrectomy. Tissue plasminogen activator is a fibrinolytic agent.

pool.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with recent onset of ptosis and occasional diplopia. Examination reveals ptosis, deficient upgaze, and pigmentary retinopathy. options.d: a mutation of mtDNA-encoded ribosomal RNA (rRNA)

The infraorbital artery, which is derived from the maxillary artery and thus is derived from the external carotid artery, provides some blood supply to the inferior oblique and inferior rectus muscles.

pool.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with proptosis and decreased vision in her left eye. Fundoscopic examination reveals optic nerve pallor OS. Perimetry reveals peripheral visual field defects OS. options.c: shearing forces in the optic canal portion
options.d: interruption of the vascular supply in the intraorbital portion

pool.rationale:
Proptosis and optic neuropathy in the setting of hyperthyroidism suggest a diagnosis of thyroid-related ophthalmopathy. There are three potential causes of optic neuropathy secondary to thyroid-related ophthalmopathy:
  1. Compression of the nerve at the orbital apex by enlarged extraocular muscle bellies
  2. Optic nerve stretch due to increased orbital volume and resultant proptosis
  3. Compression along the length of retrobulbar nerve due to orbital congestion
Of these mechanisms, only stretch is offered as an answer choice here. The intraorbital optic nerve is 25 mm to 30 mm in length, but the distance between the optic canal and the back of the globe is only 18 mm. The proptosis of thyroid-related ophthalmopathy can cause straightening of the optic nerve and stretching of the fibers, leading to optic neuropathy. Interruption of the vascular supply is not typically associated with thyroid-related ophthalmopathy. Shearing forces in the optic canal are associated with traumatic optic neuropathy. While direct compression of the nerve by large extraocular muscles may occur in the setting of thyroid-related ophthalmopathy, the location of this compression is in front of, not within, the bony canal.

pool.q: How are the ciliary body’s nonpigmented epithelial cells and pigmented epithelial cells oriented to each other?

options.b: basal side of the nonpigmented epithelial cells to basal side of the pigmented epithelial cells

pool.q: What electrophysiologic test best evaluates the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?

The c-wave of the ERG can be used to study the RPE but is not typically employed clinically. Oscillatory potentials, seen on the ERG, are responses from the inner retina that are used in the evaluation of retinal vascular disease.
Multifocal ERG is used to evaluate individual areas of the macula, and the pattern ERG focuses on retinal ganglion cell function. Visual evoked potential (VEP) measures the changes that occur at the occipital cortex following light stimulation and assesses the afferent visual system.

pool.q: What condition is characterized by a mutation in a gene encoding type II collagen, leading to premature liquefaction of vitreous with peripheral condensation that may induce retinal detachment?

pool.q: What developmental abnormality is almost always a result of mutations in the PAX6 gene?

The lacrimal glands are responsible for the aqueous layer. The meibomian glands are responsible for the oily layer. The corneal epithelial cells do not contribute to the precorneal tear film.

pool.q: What vessels perfuse the choroid?

options.c: the long and short posterior ciliary arteries

pool.rationale: The long and short posterior ciliary arteries and the perforating anterior ciliary arteries perfuse the choroid. The choroid is drained by the vortex veins. The choroid is approximately 250 microns thick and comprises 3 layers: the choriocapillaris, the middle layer of small vessels, and the outer layer of large vessels. The choriocapillaris perfuses the outer retinal layer. The anterior ciliary arteries perfuse the conjunctiva, sclera, and extraocular muscles. The central retinal artery perfuses the nerve fibers forming the optic nerve.

pool.q: The major arterial circle (MAC) is located where within the eye?
pool.rationale: The major arterial circle (MAC) is formed by the junction of the long posterior ciliary arteries and the anterior ciliary arteries. It lies within the stroma of the ciliary body near the iris root. Branches of the MAC enter the iris periphery through the iris root and have a radial orientation.

pool.q: The gene product that is defective in cases of retinoblastoma has what cellular function?
pool.rationale: The retinoblastoma protein regulates the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint and functions as a tumor suppressor. Mutations in the retinoblastoma gene (RB1) are found not only in other related tumors, such as osteosarcoma, but also in unrelated tumors such as breast cancer and lung cancer. The hereditary pattern of familial retinoblastoma is autosomal dominant. However, at the cellular level, it is autosomal recessive; a mutation on both chromosomes in a given cell is required in order for tumorigenesis to occur.

pool.q: What medication may cause increased pigmentation of the iris and periocular skin?

Betaxolol is a beta blocker, brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, and brinzolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.

options.b: It is innervated by the inferior division of cranial nerve III.

pool.q: Once activated by light, rhodopsin is finally inactivated by what chemical process?

options.a: inflow of cations into the outer segment
options.b: release of glutamate from the synaptic terminal
options.d: phosphorylation by rhodopsin kinase and binding of arrestin

pool.rationale: Rhodopsin is inactivated by its phosphorylation by rhodopsin kinase and subsequent binding of arrestin. Activation of rhodopsin causes the 11-cis-retinal double bond to be reconfigured, creating all-trans-retinal. This activates transducin, leading to a cascade that stops the inflow of cations by closing a sodium/calcium channel. The subsequent hyperpolarization of the rod stops the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitter glutamate to the corresponding bipolar cell. A signal is then generated in the bipolar cell and passed on to the ganglion cell. Within the rod photoreceptor outer segment, closure of the channel results in reduction of calcium, which activates calcium-regulated proteins and eventually rhodopsin kinase. Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates rhodopsin, which is then bound by arrestin, which deactivates rhodopsin.

pool.q: Induced corneal hypoesthesia is believed to be partially responsible for keratolysis following cataract surgery with use of what class of topical ophthalmic drugs?
pool.rationale: Keratolysis in the setting of cataract surgery is most commonly associated with preexisting tear-film abnormalities resulting from keratoconjunctivitis sicca, Sjögren syndrome, or autoimmune disease, such as rheumatoid arthritis. Postoperative use of topical nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs such as diclofenac also heightens the risk of sterile melting, through induced epithelial toxicity and corneal hypoesthesia. Corticosteroids, α2-adrenergic agonists, and fluoroquinolones are not typically associated with sterile corneal melting.

pool.q: Where are the oldest proteins in the lens located?
pool.rationale:
Fibers in the lens nucleus are laid down from embryogenesis through adolescence. Fibers are formed from epithelial cells at the lens equator; therefore, the closer the fibers are to the periphery, the younger they are.
The oldest layers, the embryonic and fetal lens nuclei, were produced in embyronic life and persist in the center of the lens. There is little if any turnover of protein in the central region of the lens (where the oldest, denucleated cells are found). The outermost layers are the most recently formed and make up the cortex of the lens.

pool.q: What type of inner nuclear layer cell is nonneural and plays a supportive role to the neural tissue extending from the inner segments of the photoreceptors to the internal limiting membrane (ILM), which is formed by their end-feet?
pool.rationale:
The inner nuclear layer has 3 classes of neurons (bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine cells) and a glial cell (the Müller cell). There are separate bipolar cells for rods and cones and at least 2 distinctly different types of cone bipolar cells: on-bipolar and off-bipolar. The horizontal cells are antagonistic interneurons that inhibit photoreceptors by releasing c-aminobutyric acid (GABA) when depolarized. Cone amacrine cells mediate antagonistic interactions among on-bipolar, off-bipolar, and ganglion cells. The rods have an unusual amacrine cell that receives the input of rod bipolar cells and delivers signals to on- and off-bipolar ganglion cells.
Müller cells are the least understood of all of the retinal cells. Nonneural, they play a supportive role to the neural tissue extending from the inner segments of the photoreceptors to the ILM, which is formed by their end-feet. They buffer the ionic concentrations in the extracellular space, seal off the subretinal space by forming the external limiting membrane (ELM), and may play a role in vitamin A metabolism in cones.

pool.q: What is the genetic principle that describes the inactivation of 1 X chromosome in every somatic cell in females?
pool.rationale:
In 1961, British geneticist Mary F. Lyon advanced the explanation for the unanticipated or partial expression of a trait in a heterozygous female, known as X-chromosome inactivtion or lyonization. This genetic concept states that in every somatic cell in a female, only 1 X chromosome is active, and the second is inactive and seen in the nuclear structure as a "Barr body." Inactivation of an X chromosome usually follows a normal distribution with 50% paternal and 50% maternal X chromosomes inactivated. However, in some cases, a mutant X may be activated in most cells, and the female may express an X-linked disorder. In ophthalmology there are rare cases of known women with X-linked ocular albinism, X-linked retinitis pigmentosa (RP), or other known X-linked disorders.
Expressivity is the variety of ways and levels of severity that a particular genetic trait manifests its presence among different affected individuals. Penetrance is the presence or absence of any effect of a gene. Polymorphism is the occurence of 2 or more alleles at a specific locus with a frequency greater than 1% each.

pool.q: Mutations of what photoreceptor-specific gene cause several retinal degenerations, ranging from autosomal dominantly inherited retinitis pigmentosa (ADRP) to pattern dystrophy and fundus flavimaculatus?
pool.rationale: There is substantial allelic heterogeneity in the peripherin/RDS gene (PRPH2) (see Table 12-2). Defects cause several dominantly inherited retinal degenerations that range from ADRP to macular degeneration, pattern macular dystrophy, vitelliform macular dystrophy, butterfly macular dystrophy, and fundus flavimaculatus. A heterozygous null mutation in a form of myosin VIIA causes Usher syndrome type I. Homozygous defects in the PEX1 gene cause infantile Refsum disease, with RP, cognitive disabilities, and hearing deficits. Homozygous defects of ornithine amino transferase (OAT) cause gyrate atrophy.

pool.q: Nonprescription vitamin supplementation has been shown to be beneficial in the management of what ocular disease?
pool.rationale: The Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) demonstrated benefit to nonprescription-based vitamin supplementation in the management of intermediate to severe nonexudative age-related macular degeneration.

pool.q: What is the maximal approximate thickness of the peripheral cornea?
pool.rationale: The central corneal thickness is approximately 500 microns (0.5 mm), which is significantly thinner than the peripheral corneal thickness of approximately 650-1000 microns. This is mostly due to the fact that the posterior surface of the cornea has a smaller radius of curvature than the anterior surface. The central cornea is steeper than the peripheral cornea. It is worth noting that there is variability in the literature regarding the thickness of the peripheral cornea, and the BCSC notes a peripheral thickness of 650-1000 microns.

pool.q: From what embryonic layer are the sphincter and dilator muscles of the iris derived?
pool.rationale: The smooth muscle of the iris and ciliary body are derived from neuroectoderm, whereas smooth muscle elsewhere in the body is derived from mesoderm. The smooth muscles of the iris respond rapidly to neuronal impulses and regulate pupil size. Smooth muscle of the iris and ciliary body is central to accommodation.

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action of moxifloxacin?
pool.rationale: Moxifloxacin is a broad-spectrum antibiotic of the fluoroquinolone class that is active against both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. It functions by inhibiting topoisomerase, an enzyme needed to separate bacterial DNA, and it thereby inhibits DNA replication. Penicillin functions by inhibiting the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links in the bacterial cell wall. Gentamicin binds to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit and thereby interferes with protein synthesis. Polymyxin binds to a negatively charged site in the lipopolysaccharide layer and thereby alters bacterial outer membrane permeability.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Fundamentals & Principles of Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An increase in tear film osmolarity is suggestive of what problem?
pool.rationale: Tear film osmolarity is one of a multitude of tests to determine the state of the ocular surface. It can be elevated in keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS, or dry eye syndrome) and is diagnostic of this condition. Osmolarity can also be increased in blepharitis and contact lens use. Other diagnostic tests for the quality of the tear film include inflammatory markers such as metalloproteinase 9 (MMP-9), as well as tear breakup time, fluorescein staining, lissamine green staining, rose bengal staining, Schirmer testing, and evaluation of the tear meniscus.

pool.q: Cycloplegia-induced psychosis is most likely to occur in what age group?
pool.rationale: Cycloplegia-induced psychosis is a dose-related complication of anticholinergic or parasympatholytic therapy. Although the elderly may be at increased risk, pediatric patients are at greatest risk because of their small body mass. Teens and young adults are at lowest risk of this complication. In most cases, cycloplegia-induced psychosis can be treated by discontinuation of the agent, but if more immediate management of flushing, fever, tachycardia, or delirium is required, these can be treated with subcutaneous physostigmine 0.25 mg every 15 minutes until symptoms subside.

pool.q: From what embryologic layer is the corneal epithelium derived?
pool.rationale: Multiple embryologic layers contribute to the development of the eye in utero. The corneal epithelium and the crystalline lens are derived from the surface ectoderm. The corneal stroma and endothelium are derived from neural crest cells. Neuroectoderm is responsible for the retinal pigmented epithelium, neurosensory retina, optic nerve, and epithelial surfaces of the iris and ciliary body. Some ocular tissue of mesodermal origin includes choroid, extraocular muscle fibers, temporal sclera, and vascular endothelium.

pool.q: Retrocorneal fibrous membrane (RCFM) forms at what location in the cornea?

options.a: posterior surface of the endothelial cells
options.b: between Bowman layer and anterior stroma
options.c: between posterior stroma and Descemet membrane
options.d: between Descemet membrane and the endothelium

pool.rationale: Infiltration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes in response to serious cornea injury induces endothelial cells to become fibroblastic and create an RCFM. The RCFM forms between Descemet membrane and the corneal endothelium and significantly compromises visual acuity.

pool.q: The nasolacrimal duct originates from what embryonic tissue?
pool.rationale: The nasolacrimal duct develops between gestation week 4 and 5 along the nasolacrimal groove between the nasal and maxillary prominence. The duct arises from ectoderm and forms the lacrimal sac at the cranial end and exits caudally at the inferior meatus. Complete canalization is usually complete around the time of birth. Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction occurs in 50% of infants at the valve of Hasner, which is the distal end of the duct. Since lacrimation does not fully develop until around 6 weeks of age, an infant with an obstruction may not show epiphora until that time.

pool.q: What part of the ocular outflow apparatus is in closest proximity to the anterior chamber?
pool.rationale: The trabecular meshwork can be divided into 3 layers: uveal meshwork, corneoscleral meshwork, and juxtacanalicular tissue. The uveal meshwork lies on the internal most portion of the trabecular meshwork and thus is in closest proximity to the anterior chamber. Aqueous filters through the trabecular meshwork into the Schlemm canal and then into 25-30 collector channels that arise from the Schlemm canal before draining into the deep, midscleral, and episcleral venous plexuses.

pool.q: What posterior segment structure, if inflamed, would be considered uveitis?
pool.rationale: The uveal tract is the main vascular compartment of the eye and consists of the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. The optic nerve, cornea, and retinal pigment epithelium are not part of the uvea.

pool.q: Where is the germinative zone of the lens epithelium located?

options.a: at the equator of the lens
options.b: immediately posterior to the lens equator
options.c: immediately anterior to the lens equator
options.d: at the apical center of the lens

On a side note, the lens capsule is thinnest posteriorly, with a thickness of 3–5 microns.

pool.q: What characteristic of the retina makes it more vulnerable to damage from lipid peroxidation?

options.a: high number of mitochondria in the rod inner segments
options.b: high levels of saturated fatty acids in the rod outer segments
options.c: poor oxygen supply through the choroid

pool.rationale: The retina has several distinctive characteristics that make it vulnerable to damage from lipid peroxidation. (1) Rod inner segments are rich in mitochondria, which may leak activated oxygen species. (2) Rod outer segments possess high levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), making them susceptible to damage by oxygen. PUFAs are sensitive to peroxidation in proportion to their number of double bonds. (3) The abundant oxygen supply through the choroid and retinal vessels elevates the risk of oxidative damage. (4) There are many chromophores in the outer retina. Light exposure may trigger photooxidative processes mediated by singlet oxygen, and the RPE may play a key role.

pool.q: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) act to prevent prostaglandin formation via inhibition of what enzyme?

The other enzymes listed (thromboxane synthetase, prostaglandin isomerases, lipoxygenase) are in the prostaglandin production pathway but are not the target of NSAID activity; however, they may be affected by other pharmaceutical agents.

pool.q: Retinal nerve fibers corresponding to what part of the retina cross posteriorly in the chiasm?
pool.rationale: The extramacular fibers from the inferonasal retina cross anteriorly in the chiasm at the “Wilbrand knee” before passing into the optic tract (thus accounting for the development of a junctional scotoma with a lesion affecting the "junction" of the optic nerve and chiasm). Extramacular superonasal fibers cross directly to the opposite tract. Extramacular temporal fibers remain uncrossed in the chiasm and optic tract. The macular projections are located centrally in the optic nerve and constitute 80%–90% of the total volume of the optic nerve and the chiasmal fibers. The temporal macular fibers pursue a direct course through the chiasm as a bundle of uncrossed fibers. Nasal macular fibers cross in the posterior part of the chiasm. This unique anatomy can lead to a macular, or central, bitemporal hemianopia in a compressive lesion abutting the posterior chiasm, such as a pituitary adenoma with a prefixed chiasm.

pool.q: The anterior layer of the tear film is secreted primarily by the meibomian glands but secondarily by what other glands?

The sebaceous glands of Zeis, located at the eyelid margin close to the eyelash roots, also secrete lipid, which is incorporated into the tear film. The glands of Krause and Wolfring are both accessory lacrimal glands that contribute to the aqueous layer of the tear film. Tear film mucins are secreted mainly by the conjunctival goblet cells and stratified squamous cells of the conjunctiva and cornea epithelium and minimally by the lacrimal glands of Henle and Manz.

pool.q: In the evaluation of a scleral wound following trauma, it is important to measure the full extent of the lesion. What external landmark of the eye gives the approximate location of the ora serrata?

options.a: entrance of the anterior ciliary arteries through the sclera
options.b: insertion of the 4 rectus muscle tendons
options.c: insertion of the inferior oblique tendon
options.d: insertion of the superior oblique tendon

pool.rationale:
The 4 rectus muscles insert anteriorly on the globe (Figure 1). The medial rectus tendon inserts most anteriorly, approximately 5.5 mm from the limbus, followed by the inferior rectus tendon (6.5 mm) and the lateral rectus tendon (6.9 mm). The superior rectus inserts most posteriorly, approximately 7.7 mm from the limbus. An imaginary line drawn externally between the rectus muscle insertions forms the spiral of Tillaux and approximates the internal location of the ora serrata (Figure 2). This is clinically important because a suture passed through the full thickness of the sclera posterior to this line could penetrate the retina. Further, a scleral laceration or rupture that extends beyond the muscle insertion corresponds with a worse visual prognosis.
The superior oblique tendon inserts superotemporally, below the superior rectus, just posterior to the globe equator. The inferior oblique tendon also inserts in the posterior sclera (behind the equator) in the inferotemporal quadrant, overlying the macula. The anterior ciliary arteries branch from the ophthalmic artery. The branches pass through the belly of each rectus muscle, penetrate the sclera, anastomose with the major arterial circle, and contribute to the blood supply of the anterior segment. These arteries enter the sclera just outside the limbus.

pool.q: Arterial blood supply to the whole uveal tract, the sclera, the margin of the cornea, and the adjacent conjunctiva is provided by what arteries?

A single anterior ciliary artery enters the lateral rectus from the lacrimal artery. The posterior ciliary arteries also arise from the ophthalmic artery and supply the whole uveal tract, the cilioretinal arteries, the sclera, the margin of the cornea, and adjacent conjunctiva. The 2 long ciliary arteries enter the sclera on either side of the optic nerve and travel a short distance in the suprachoroidal space. There are no lateral ciliary arteries.

pool.q: What is the peak sensitivity of rhodopsin?
pool.rationale: The retina consists of 3 cone pigments and 1 rod pigment. The rod’s visual pigment is rhodopsin, which absorbs green light best at a wavelength of approximately 510 nm. It absorbs blue and yellow light less well and is insensitive to longer wavelengths (red light).

pool.q: You are in the operating room to repair a ruptured globe. You identify a full-thickness scleral laceration that starts at the inferior limbus and extends posteriorly to the insertion of the inferior rectus. What is your best estimate of how long the laceration is?

The muscle closest to the limbus is the medial rectus (5.5 mm). From here, as you head inferiorly, the muscles "spiral" out with increasing distances from the limbus: inferior rectus (6.5mm), lateral rectus (6.9 mm), and superior rectus (7.7 mm). There is some variation in the exact distances, but of the answer choices given, the only plausible one for the inferior rectus is 6.5 mm.

pool.q: A 63-year-old man presents with painless vision loss in the left eye for an unknown amount of time. Visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. Visual field testing revealed the finding shown. What is the most appropriate imaging modality to evaluate his vision loss?
pool.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for evaluation of the central nervous system (CNS). pool.q: The retinal pigment epithelium is derived from what embryonic layer?

options.b: surface ectoderm, inner layer of the optic cup
options.c: neuroectoderm, inner layer of the optic cup
options.d: neuroectoderm, outer layer of the optic cup

pool.rationale:
Embryology can be difficult to retain but also helpful in understanding the basis of abnormalities in the formed eye. In the first 2 weeks after fertilization, the zygote divides to form a 16-cell morula. The morula then forms a cystic blastula. The blastula contains a small inner mass of cells called the embryoblast, which will become the embryo. The cells that line the cystic portion of the blastula form the trophoblast, which will become the placenta and support tissues. The embryoblast divides into 2 layers of cells, the epiblast and hypoblast. The majority of the epiblast will become ectoderm, but some of the cells migrate in between the epiblast and hypoblast layers to form mesoderm. These mesenchymal cells form the notochord, a primitive axial skeleton. The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to differentiate into neuroectoderm (neural plate). The brain and eye develop from the most anterior portion of the neural plate.
The neural plate begins to fold inward. The cells at the apex of these neural folds become the neural crest cells. The neural folds close to form a neural tube with overlying surface ectoderm. As the neural tube closes, optic pits develop from the anterior portion (now the forebrain vesicle). The optic pits deepen and become the optic vesicles. As the optic vesicle approaches the outer wall of the embryo, there is a focal thickening of the surface ectoderm (the lens placode). The lens placode invaginates to form the lens vesicle. Simultaneously, the optic vesicle invaginates within itself to form a 2-layered optic cup. The outer layer of the optic cup will become a monolayer of retinal pigment epithelium. The inner invaginated layer of the optic cup will become neurosensory retina.

Pericytes surround the endothelial cells and are modified smooth muscle cells that play a role in autoregulation of retinal blood vessels. Amacrine cells are inhibitory interneurons that mediate interactions among bipolar and ganglion cells.

Outside the fovea, the radial fibers maintain an orthogonal orientation to the ILM.
The inner nuclear layer (INL) contains nuclei of the bipolar, Müller, horizontal, and amacrine cells. The inner plexiform layer (IPL) comprises axons of the bipolar and amacrine cells and dendrites of the ganglion cells and their synapses. Photoreceptor nuclei are located in the outer nuclear layer (ONL).

pool.q: What is the recommendation from the AAO Task Force on Genetic Testing regarding genetic testing of asymptomatic minors?

options.a: Avoid testing minors for asymptomatic, untreatable disorders except in extraordinary circumstances.
options.b: Offer routine genetic testing to the parents for genetically complex disorders in all circumstances.
options.c: Use a local laboratory for clinical testing in order to avoid unnecessary costs to the parents.
options.d: Encourage parents to use direct-to-consumer genetic testing initially for screening purposes.

pool.rationale:
The 7 recommendations from the AAO Task Force on Genetic Testing are:
  1. Offer genetic testing to patients who have clinical findings of a mendelian disorder for which a causative gene or genes have been identified.
  2. Use Clinical Laboratories Improvement Amendments (CLIA)-approved laboratories for all clinical testing.
  3. Provide a copy of each genetic test report to the patient so that she or he will be able independently to seek mechanism-specific information.
  4. Avoid use of direct-to-consumer genetic testing and discourage patients from obtaining such tests themselves.
  5. Avoid unnecessary parallel testing; order the most specific test(s) available given the patient's clinical findings.
  6. Avoid routine genetic testing for genetically complex disorders, such as age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) and late-onset primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), until specific treatment or surveillance strategies have been shown in one or more published clinical trials to be of benefit to individuals with specific disease-associated genotypes.

pool.q: From what vessel does the vascular supply to the lacrimal gland originate?

The ophthalmic branch (CN V1) of the trigeminal nerve delivers sensory innervation to the lacrimal gland.

pool.q: In what quadrant is a chorioretinal coloboma most likely to be found?

The location of the fissure closure correlates with the inferonasal quadrant, which is where colobomas are typically found. Therefore, bilateral optic nerve and/or chorioretinal coloboma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of bitemporal hemianopsia.

pool.q: Levels of what enzyme have been shown to be elevated in patients with severe disorders affecting the ocular surface, including Sjögren syndrome and graft-vs-host disease, as well as in patients after laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?

pool.q: What supplement would interfere with prescribing oral doxycycline, rifampin, and high-dose prednisone to a patient for disseminated bartonellosis and neuroretinitis?

The standard B-scan probe positions are transverse, longitudinal, and axial.
Coronal, radial, and tangential are not standard B-scan probe positions.

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin type A?

pool.q: A 38-year-old male who is a brittle Type 1 diabetic is referred for evaluation of decreased vision, progressive over the past 3 months and painless. The patient states that before the onset of these symptoms his vision was "good," and that he has had no diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy on annual examinations in the past (his last dilated examination was 5 months ago), but his latest HbA1c level is 11.2. What is the most likely finding on anterior segment examination, based on this presentation?
pool.rationale:
True diabetic cataract is a rapidly developing, bilateral "snowflake" cataract that appears in the lens cortex of patients with poorly controlled Type 1 DM. Typically people with Type 2 DM do not develop this type of cataract, but they do have a higher prevalence of age-related cataract with slightly earlier onset than the general population. Animal models show that those with DM (either natural or induced) develop cataracts that are associated with the presence of sorbitol in the lens and with the influx of water. The osmotic hypothesis may account for these findings, which states that aldose reductase serves to increase the sorbitol content of the lens. Sorbitol is unable to penetrate cell membranes and is then trapped inside the cells, creating an osmotic gradient that draws water into the lens, swelling the cells. This damages cell membranes, leading to cataract formation.
Keratic precipitates would indicate a uveitic process, which is unlikely in this scenario. Neovascularization of the iris can be a sign of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which would not be as likely for this patient, given his recent "normal" fundus exam. Telangiectatic/corkscrew vessels in the episclera could indicate elevated episcleral venous pressure, which would not generally be seen in Type 1 DM alone.

pool.q: Alterations in glucose metabolism can result in cataract formation. Under normal physiologic conditions, what is the primary pathway by which glucose is converted into adenosine triphosphate (ATP) in the human lens?

options.d: hexose monophosphate shunt (also called pentose phosphate pathway)

pool.rationale:
Normally, glucose enters the lens via diffusion from the aqueous humor and is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate before passing through glycolysis to generate ATP.  This provides the majority of the energy for the lens. Hexokinase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the glycolytic pathway.
Due to the poor oxygen saturation in the lens, aerobic metabolism is not possible.
A small amount of glucose-6-phosphate enters the hexose monophosphate shunt (also called pentose phosphate pathway). This pathway is responsible for replenishing nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) stores, which are depleted by redox reactions.
The polyol pathway (also called sorbitol-aldose reductase pathway) becomes important in the setting of hyperglycemia, in which glucose is metabolized through the polyol pathway and sorbitol is generated. Sorbitol does not readily traverse cell membranes, and its accumulation is thought to play a role in the development of sugar cataracts.

pool.q: While isolating rectus muscles during routine strabismus surgery, the anesthesiologist reports that the patient is experiencing severe bradycardia. What is the preferred initial management?

options.a: Administer additional retrobulbar anesthesia while the assistant infraducts the eye.
options.b: Continue working while the anesthesiologist administers intravenous atropine.
options.c: Release any tension on the muscle and monitor for improved heart rate.
options.d: Finish isolating muscles as quickly as possible and recheck vital signs.

pool.rationale:
This scenario describes the oculocardiac reflex, which is a decline in heart rate due to traction on the conjunctiva, globe, or extraocular muscles, particularly the medial rectus. Asystole is the most severe form of the oculocardiac reflex. If muscles will be manipulated during a case, the surgeon must keep this in mind, and the anesthesiologist should be notified. If a patient has significant bradycardia, the surgeon should be prepared to release any traction on the muscle(s) immediately.
Retrobulbar anesthesia, once achieved, can prevent the afferent end of the reflex, but the oculocardiac reflex may occur during administration of the block. Intravenous atropine can be administered to protect against bradycardia, but release of tension on the muscle is the first step.

pool.q: What type of collagen production is associated uniquely with corneal stromal wound healing?
pool.rationale: Type I is the major collagen component of the corneal stroma; it constitutes approximately 70% of the total stromal dry weight. Immunohistochemical and biochemical studies have shown that normal adult corneal stroma also contains collagen types V, VI, VII, XII, and XIV.  Type III collagen production is associated uniquely with stromal wound healing.
